t: The Nazca lived in the river valleys of Peru’s southern desert from about 100 BCE to 800 CE, farming with water drawn from underground channels, several dozen of which still work.
Their ceremonial centre at Cahuachi drew whole villages to feasts, where people received the fine painted pottery that carried Nazca images of gods and mythical beings.
They made the Nazca Lines, vast figures and lines on the desert floor whose purpose is still debated, and declined after about 500 CE amid floods and erosion.
dyk: Some Nazca burials have a “head jar” in place of the missing head: a pot painted with a human face, sometimes with plants sprouting from it.
ev: Nazca culture emerges from the Paracas culture on the southern coast of Peru
In the Early Nazca period, the mounds and plazas of Cahuachi are the centre of ritual and feasting
Around the end of Nazca phase 3 or start of phase 4 Cahuachi is abandoned, probably after a drought across the Andes
In the Middle Nazca period the puquios, underground aqueducts, are built
Power shifts from the coast to the highlands with the rise of the Wari culture
Nazca culture has fallen, probably after El Niño floods on a landscape stripped of trees

f.homeland: The arid southern coast of Peru: the river valleys of the Río Grande de Nazca drainage and the Ica Valley, in today’s Ica Region; key sites the ceremonial centre of Cahuachi and the puquios of Cantalloc
f.period: Proto Nazca c. 100 BCE–1 CE; Early Nazca c. 1–450 CE; Middle Nazca c. 450–550 CE; Late Nazca c. 550–750 CE; in decline from c. 500 CE and fallen by c. 750 CE
f.known: the Nazca Lines; puquios, underground aqueducts still in use; polychrome pottery in at least twelve colours; textiles; the ceremonial centre of Cahuachi; trophy heads; trephination and shaped skulls
f.sources: excavations at Cahuachi and other sites; burials preserved by the dry desert; the nine-phase pottery sequence; ceramic and textile iconography; chemical study of clays; AMS dating of rock varnish in the puquios
